### Command palette (⌘K)
- **⌘K palette** — `cmdk`-based fuzzy command palette in a top-anchored `ModalShell`; ⌘K toggles, Esc closes. _Support:_ `src/components/CommandPalette.tsx`. _Entry:_ ⌘K.
- **Talk group (#1153)** — After Workspaces and Groups, with an active workspace (`data-tour="palette-talk"`): **New conversation** (`⌘⌥N`), **Switch conversation…** (`⌘⌥K`; opens the conversation switcher), while a conversation is open, **Copy conversation as Markdown** (the Chats row's export), and, while an approval card waits in the conversation Talk shows, **Focus the waiting approval card** (`⌘⌥A`; the oldest one, a frame after the palette closes and hands the focus back to its opener). Each one shows Talk first. _Support:_ `CommandPalette.tsx` (`talk`), wired in `App.tsx`; `CommandPalette.talk.test.tsx`.
- **Groups** — **Sessions** (New session, Switch to <session>, Kill active); **Workspaces** (one row per non-archived workspace across every open project in the rail: the workspace name over a mono `<project> · <branch>` meta line (`<project> · <group> · <branch>` for a mission in a mission group, outermost first like the slim rail's flyout; when every listed workspace belongs to one project the line leaves the project out and reads `<branch>` / `<group> · <branch>`, so the branch's distinguishing middle and tail get the whole width — `paletteShowsProject` / `paletteWorkspaceMeta` in `src/lib/paletteWorkspaces.ts`, #935), both middle-truncated with `MidTruncate` like the rail and kept whole, project included, in a tooltip, the rail's monogram glyph (`resolveMonogram`: the custom glyph, else the name's initial) in the row's glyph box; each row's cmdk `value` is the workspace id (prefixed `ws:`), so two same-named workspaces (a `main` in each of two same-named projects) stay distinct rows for the arrow keys, and its `keywords` carry the name, branch, project and mission group, so typing part of a branch or a project name finds it, and a group's name finds its missions (as a group-name hit keeps a group's members in the rail filter). The palette's `filter` (`paletteFilter`) scores a `ws:` row on those keywords only, never on the id: a UUID would otherwise let any query of hex letters and digits (`772`, `dec`) fuzzy-match most workspaces; every other row keeps cmdk's `defaultFilter`. Order: workspaces whose crew needs you first — a paused run in `runsStore.runsByWs`, the Dock badge's `needsYou` rule — longest-waiting first by `statusSince`, then workspaces something is working in (the rail's `runningByWs`: chat, Direct run, busy terminal, live shell), then the rest by most recent `lastActive`, ties by name in natural order (`Intl.Collator` with `numeric: true`, so *rollout-3* comes before *rollout-10*, #967). A static 5px dot in a reserved slot says *Needs you* (brass, the rail's non-beacon dot) or *Working* (sage), with a title; the palette never pulses. Selecting a row switches project and workspace exactly like a rail click (`App.handleSelectWorkspace`). No new shortcut; ⌘1…⌘9 still cover only the active project. `data-tour="palette-workspaces"` on the group. _Support:_ `lib/paletteWorkspaces.ts`); **Groups** (after Workspaces at rest; **before** them once a query is typed, since a group's name also finds its missions and the group is then the likelier target; the order is the JSX's, as cmdk 1.1 sorts rows within a section but never the sections, and the two sections are one keyed list, so the first keystroke moves the Groups section instead of remounting it; one row per rail group of the open projects, in the rail's reading order: a project group, then the mission groups of its projects, then a loose project's mission groups (`paletteGroups` in `lib/paletteGroups.ts`, over `layoutProjects`); a mission group of a project that isn't open is left out. Each row: the group's chevron in its tint (mute untinted) in the glyph box, the name over a mono meta line — `<project> · N missions` for a mission group, `N projects` for a project group, `empty` for either with no members — both middle-truncated; the row's title names the kind (`Mission group: Fixes`). Its cmdk `value` is `group:<id>`, scored on its keywords only (the name, plus the project's name for a mission group). Choosing a row closes the palette and **reveals the group in the rail** (`revealGroup` → `railGroupUiStore.requestReveal`): the slim rail opens to 280px, the group's project group, its project (for a mission group) and the group itself unfold, a rail filter that hides it is cleared, and the header is scrolled into view and focused a frame later (after the palette hands its focus back), where its own keys take over (`F2` rename, `⇧F10` menu, `←`/`→` fold). The palette renames and moves nothing itself: it has no sub-steps or text entry for an action (its one action that asks is a native prompt), so group actions stay in the rail's menus and keys. `data-tour="palette-groups"`); **Models** (one row per model, labelled with its bare name, hot-swaps the active session's agent; with no query the group is a short preview of three — the active session's model first, then the catalogue order — and a `⋯` **Show all models** row (`N more`, `data-tour="palette-models-more"`) reveals the rest in place without closing the palette, so a long model list never pushes Workspaces and Actions down; typing searches every model exactly as before (`lib/paletteModels.ts`, `MODEL_PREVIEW`); choosing **Show all models** (Enter or click) moves the selection onto the first model it revealed (`firstRevealedModel`), never back to the palette's first row (#897), and a held Enter acts once: the palette's `onKeyDown` prevents a repeated Enter, so key repeat never runs that model's switch (#908); the palette's cmdk selection is controlled, each model row's `value` is `model:<provider>/<id>` with its name and provider as `keywords` (`paletteFilter` scores a `model:` row on those keywords only, like a `ws:` row), and the selection is parked on the last shown model before the row unmounts (`flushSync`) so cmdk never re-selects "New session", then the first revealed row is selected through cmdk's own pointer selection once it is mounted, so the input's and the list's `aria-activedescendant` point at it, not at the removed row (a controlled `value` change alone moves `aria-selected` but not cmdk's active descendant); the query, the preview and the selection reset when the palette closes, so a reopen never paints the old state for a frame (#897); the provider · price meta ellipsizes before the name does and keeps its full text in a tooltip — true of every row's meta); **Templates** (session templates → new-session flow); **Actions** (Open a pull request ⌘⇧P — only with an active workspace, Import a crew… (opens the crew import review sheet), Check for updates, What's new, Preview unreleased tips (dev builds only), Open Settings · Usage ⌘⇧T, Set token budget, Export session JSON/CSV); **Editor** (toggle word wrap, font ±, cycle tab width, toggle line numbers, toggle blame); **Themes** (Theme: <name>). _Support:_ `CommandPalette.tsx`; `sessionStore`, `ipc.switchAgent`, `updaterStore`, `editorPrefsStore`, `blameStore`, `themeStore`. _Entry:_ ⌘K. Empty: "Nothing matches."

### Workspace search palette
- **⌘P fuzzy file finder** — Lists every non-ignored workspace file (loaded once per open) and ranks it client-side with our own matcher (cmdk's filtering is off). A query with `*`, `?`, `[`, `\` or a `{a,b}` group is a **glob**: without a `/` it matches the file name (`*.java`, `User*Test.kt`), with a `/` the whole path (`src/**/*.ts`; `**/` spans zero or more directories). **Braces** expand bash-style, nested too (`*.{ts,tsx}`, `{Foo,Bar}.java`), and each alternative matches the name or the path on its own (`{src/lib/*,README}.{ts,md}`); a `{` with no comma (`{id}`) is literal. **`\` escapes** the next character, in or out of a class (`\*.ts` finds a file literally named `*.ts`; `[\]]`). `?` and classes take one code point (`?.md` matches `😀.md`; an emoji built from several code points, like a flag or a skin tone, takes one `?` per code point: `??.md` matches `👍🏽.md`). Globs are matched by our own bit-parallel automaton (no regex, no backtracking), so time is linear in the path length for any pattern (`*a*a*a*a*b` included); its worst case grows with the square of the pattern length, so a query over 256 characters, or whose braces expand past 32 alternatives or 1,024 characters, is matched as fuzzy text instead (tested: a 256-character `**/**/…*.ts` over 20,000 paths takes under 200 ms). A malformed glob never throws: a backwards range (`[z-a]`) matches nothing, an unclosed `[` is literal. Not supported: extglobs (`+(a|b)`), POSIX classes (`[[:alpha:]]`) and brace ranges (`{1..3}`, which has no comma, so it is literal). Otherwise it is **fuzzy**, scored fzf-style — bonuses for matching in the file name, at word / camel-case boundaries (`edpn` → `EditorPane.tsx`) and in consecutive runs, plus a bonus when a term is the whole file name or its stem (`user` puts `User.java` above `UserService.java`); space-separated terms must all match (`user service`). Smart case: any capital makes the query case-sensitive. Query and paths are compared in NFC, and case is folded per character so scores line up (`İ` included). A leading `./` and the absolute workspace root are stripped, so pasted paths match. A trailing **`:line[:col]`** (`Foo.java:42`) opens the file with the caret there (the row shows the brass `:line`; a line or column past 2,147,483,647 is clamped to it); a bare `:42` names no file and is treated as the empty query, and a trailing `:` typed on the way (`index.ts:`) keeps the matches for `index.ts`. Equal scores go to open editor tabs, then to files recently opened from the finder (session-only, 50 per workspace), then the shorter path. The list is **virtualized** (fixed 30px rows, only the rows in view are in the DOM) with its own ↑/↓/Enter selection (wrapping; the selected row gets the `brass-ghost` background, and the input, which keeps focus, carries `aria-activedescendant` / `aria-controls`). Ranking is **chunked**: `createMatchJob` scores and sorts 2,048 files per unit and then merges the sorted chunks, and the palette runs units in 8 ms slices, yielding between them. The previous ranking stays on screen until the new one finishes, so no single pass over 20,000 paths blocks a keystroke for a frame (tested: the slowest unit is under 16 ms, and seven pathological globs over 20,000 60-character paths take under 200 ms in total). Enter before the ranking catches up finishes it at once and opens the top match for what was typed. Empty states: "Scanning workspace…" while listing, "No matching files.", "No files in this workspace.", and a rouge "Couldn't list the files in this workspace: …" when the listing fails. When the listing hit the backend's 20,000-file cap, the palette's footer says **"Showing the first 20,000 files"**. Selecting opens the file in the in-app editor. _Support:_ `src/components/WorkspaceSearchPalette.tsx`; `src/lib/fileMatch.ts` (`parseQuery`, `expandBraces`, `compileGlob`, `foldCase`, `scoreTerm`, `createMatchJob`, `matchFiles`); `src/stores/recentFilesStore.ts`; `editorStore.openFile(…, line, col)`; `ipc.listWorkspaceFiles`. _Entry:_ ⌘P; tour surface `file-finder`.
- **⌘⇧F workspace text search** — Server-side literal substring scan across every text file (debounced 180ms); results show file, `:line` (brass), and a preview. Selecting a hit opens the file **with the caret on that line**, centred — the palette hands the line to `navigateToFile`, which routes it through the editor's one-shot reveal. (Picking a hit used to open the file at line 1, leaving the reader to find the match again by hand.) File mode passes no line, so re-opening an already-open tab leaves the cursor where it was. _Support:_ `WorkspaceSearchPalette.tsx`; `App.navigateToFile`; `editorStore.pendingReveal`; `ipc.searchWorkspaceText`. _Entry:_ ⌘⇧F.
- **Tab toggles modes** — Tab switches Files↔Text preserving the query. The mode is named by a brass mono prefix at the start of the search line (`FILES` / `TEXT`, `data-tour="file-finder-mode"`), which is also a button that switches mode (title "Search text instead (Tab)" / "Find files instead (Tab)"); there is no tab strip and no count, since the list itself shows the results. A hairline footer holds the cap notice (files mode, only at the cap) and, on the right, where Tab goes: "Tab · search text" / "Tab · find files" (`data-tour="file-finder-tab-hint"`). _Support:_ `WorkspaceSearchPalette.tsx`. _Entry:_ Tab inside the palette, or the mode prefix.

### Onboarding / welcome / empty states
- **Welcome screen (prompt-first)** — Pre-project landing: **The Octo** hero mark (116px, `state="idle"`), "Octopush" wordmark in Fraunces (`.brand-wordmark`), "an atelier for agentic developers" tagline, a radial brass background wash, then the **prompt genesis** centerpiece (see below): a serif-placeholder textarea *"Describe what you want to build…"* + the honest promise line + an editable derived project name + the screen's one primary serif CTA **"Set a crew on it"** (Enter submits, ⇧Enter newlines; `data-tour="genesis-begin"`), always in the ceremonial frame (brass-dim border, brass-ghost fill, serif; `GENESIS_CTA_CLASS`), never a sage ghost outline — only its ink changes (see the pre-flight below). Under it, every secondary route on **one quiet line**, all in one ink (sage, ivory on hover; mute while disabled) with the same brass-tinted underline (`GENESIS_LINK_CLASS`): "or think it through first" · the demoted project-first routes **"Begin a new study"** (`data-tour="welcome-new-study"`) · **"open one from disk"** (reveals the path field; its tooltip says a folder can also be dropped anywhere on the window) — then Recent (up to 5) + "⟲ Recently closed". _Support:_ `src/components/WelcomeScreen.tsx`; `icons/OctoMark.tsx`; `lib/genesis.ts`; `projectStore`. _Entry:_ launch with no current project.
- **Prompt genesis (start from a prompt, no repo) — free** — The reframe's conclusion: intent before the **repo**. A user with an idea but no git project types what they want to build; Octopush is born from the prompt. The chain (all reused except a `task` param): `deriveProjectName(prompt)` (local slug heuristic, editable — no LLM, so it works before any key) → `create_project(location, name, task=prompt)` in a **visible `~/Octopush/`** ("it's mine, on my disk") — folder + `git init` + baseline commit + **main workspace whose task IS the prompt** → the M1 pairing titles the auto-paired `build` mission with the prompt → the app mounts the shell, resolves the **Greenfield** builtin pipeline (the crew that knows how to be born into an empty repo — see §4; falls back to Feature Factory), and **stages a crew at the Direct launcher** with the prompt as the brief (the same workspace-scoped `setLauncherPrefill` FirstRunInvite uses) — one consent click ("Begin the run") and the crew builds. No key configured → the crew is staged (prefill survives) and Settings·Models opens with an honest toast; the prompt is never lost. Dir collisions never clobber (`resolve_free_project_dir` suffixes `-2`/`-3` over a non-empty dir, adopts an empty one). **Honesty:** the copy promises *"a first working slice — you direct every gate"*, never a finished app. **Sandboxed by default:** a genesis project's mission is created with `exec_isolation = "sandbox"` (`create_project` sets it when a task is present) — a crew building a brand-new project you're not watching should be write-confined. The build-capable seatbelt profile (see §4 sandbox — package-manager caches redirected into a confined temp, no global-dir exposure) covers common toolchains; if a build needs to write outside the workspace, the failure is legible and the sandbox is a one-click **toggle-off** in the launcher foot (free, everyone). **Zero new tables/keys/migrations.** _Support:_ `commands::create_project` (+ `task`), `ensure_main_workspace` (+ `task`), `resolve_free_project_dir`; `App.handleGenesis`; `WelcomeScreen` genesis block; `lib/genesis.ts` (`deriveProjectName`, `GENESIS_PROMISE`); reuses `runsStore.setLauncherPrefill`, `firstRunStore.crewProviderReady`. Both doors coexist forever — project-first is byte-identical. Also reachable from the **New-project wizard** ("From a prompt" card — see above). _Entry:_ Welcome → the prompt textarea → "Set a crew on it"; or Rail → Add project → "From a prompt". Genesis stages the **Greenfield** crew (§4). **Pre-flight (G4):** the genesis block (`GenesisPrompt`, shared Welcome + wizard) owns a **model line** ("crew runs on {model}" — a Listbox of the configured Anthropic models; default = the crew's own, applied as launcher overrides across the pipeline's api stages) and, for a **cold user with no key**, an **inline Anthropic-key field** (masked; "Paste an Anthropic API key to wake the crew" + "Stored locally in `~/.octopush` — never leaves your machine"), (`data-tour="genesis-key-save"`; Enter saves it). The field has **no button of its own** — the block keeps one primary CTA: with a key typed and no brief yet it reads **"Wake the crew"** and only saves the key; otherwise it is "Set a crew on it" ("Waking the crew…" while saving). The CTA keeps its ceremonial frame (brass-dim border, brass-ghost fill) in every state and never dims as a whole; its ink is full brass (`GENESIS_CTA_INK_PRIMED`, `data-primed`) only when it can act with confidence — a brief plus a stored or typed key, or a key alone to save ("Wake the crew") — and receded otherwise (`GENESIS_CTA_INK_RECEDED`): sage ink for a brief with no key, where it stays clickable (the fallback below) and still clears WCAG AA on its frame in every theme, and brass/50 while disabled with nothing to submit. Saving the key goes through the **same** path Settings·Models uses (`saveAnthropicKey` → `save_providers` enable + `save_settings` merge — one key writer, no second source of truth; `save_providers` now reloads the in-memory router so the just-enabled provider is visible immediately), re-checks readiness, and the model picker appears. Submitting with a **typed-but-unsaved** key persists it first (Enter or the CTA — the whole gesture completes without the Settings detour); a user who types **no** key still proceeds and hits the honest G1 Settings·Models fallback (a keyless crew genuinely can't run).
- **Think it through first — the Sketchbook (G5) — free** — Start *without* building. Under the genesis block, "or think it through first" opens the **Sketchbook** — a real, auto-provisioned git project at `~/.octopush/sketchbook` (`ensure_sketchbook`, find-or-create by canonical path; a normal project in every way, so notes/specs are versioned for free) — and lands you in **Talk** on a fresh thread whose first message IS your prompt. No repo of your own yet, no crew spend to consent (a normal BYOK Talk turn). This is the reframe's answer to "design missions": you think in a scratch project's Talk and promote to a real project when ready (both genesis doors stay available anytime; the plan's `workspace_id=NULL` design-mission surface is **retired** in favor of this — zero new artifact surface, zero special Rail state). Keyless users stay on the Welcome (the prompt is preserved in the textarea) and are pointed to Settings·Models — a sketch is a real BYOK Talk turn. _Support:_ `commands::ensure_sketchbook`, `App.handleSketch` (readiness check → open Sketchbook → main workspace → fresh thread **before** the canvas mounts so it isn't raced → Talk → send the prompt), `GenesisPrompt` "or think it through first" (a sage serif link, ivory on hover, underlined in brass/40, and mute while disabled until there is a brief — `GENESIS_LINK_CLASS`, the same treatment as "Begin a new study", which hosts pass in through the `links` prop so they share its quiet line; `data-tour="genesis-sketch"`), `ipc.ensureSketchbook`. _Entry:_ the "or think it through first" link in **both** the Welcome and the New-project wizard genesis blocks. **Promote a sketch — "Make it a project":** the Talk Companion shows a serif **"Make it a project"** CTA **only** when the active project is the Sketchbook (`onMakeProject`, wired by App via an **exact** path match against the read-only `sketchbook_path` command — so a project opened from a subfolder inside the Sketchbook never false-matches). Clicking it seeds genesis with the thread's **first user message** as the brief (`App.handleMakeProject` → `handleGenesis`; it loads history first if the thread was reached from the Rail, so the seed is never falsely empty) — the anti-task-manager frontier: a sketch becomes execution or stays a document. (Carrying the sketch's fuller notes into the new repo is a later refinement; the seed prompt is enough to start.)
- **Post-build rename (G6) — free** — The arc's close: a genesis project is born with an anonymous heuristic slug (`ios-track-daily-tasks`), but once its **first crew ships**, the built thing knows what it is. `create_project` stamps a durable marker on a prompt-born project (`app_meta` `genesis_prompt:{id}`, only when a `task` is present — so project-first projects are never touched). A one-shot run-completion listener (`initGenesisRename`, sibling of crew notifications) fires on the project's first run reaching `completed`: it **atomically claims** the rename via the backend `claim_genesis_rename(workspace_id)` (returns the prompt only if the project is prompt-born AND not yet offered, setting the offered marker in the SAME lock — so two runs of one project completing at once can't both offer), generates a **short name via a brief BYOK call** (`ai_complete` on the fast helper model, `claude-haiku-5-5`, kebab-slugged — falls back to the local heuristic if the call fails), and shows a **quiet toast with a Rename action** ("Your crew built it. Rename it to `task-tracker`?"). Accept → `update_project_customization` (+ reflects in the open project / recent list; a null tint is a no-op, never a wipe). The claim itself is the one-shot mark, so accept or dismiss it never fires again. Never automatic, never on a project-first project (they carry no `genesis_prompt` marker); the Sketchbook is never a candidate (`ensure_sketchbook` bypasses `create_project`). _Support:_ `commands::{create_project (marker), claim_genesis_rename}`, `db::claim_genesis_rename` (atomic check-and-set), `GenesisRenameCandidate`; `src/lib/genesisRename.ts` (`initGenesisRename`/`maybeOffer`/`slugifyName`), `Toast.action` (new optional toast action button). _Entry:_ automatic, once, after a genesis project's first crew completes.
- **Folder drag-and-drop open** — Dropping a folder reads its path and opens it. _Support:_ `WelcomeScreen.tsx`. _Entry:_ drag a folder onto the welcome screen.
- **New-project flow** — `NewProjectFlow` full-screen when no project, or as an overlay over the current project from the rail's "Add project". _Support:_ `App.tsx`; `WorkspaceRail.onAddProject`. _Entry:_ Welcome CTA / rail add-project.
- **First-run crew invite (one-shot)** — The differentiator's minute-one moment: a new user who has **never started a Direct run** sees a one-shot card floating over the **Talk canvas** (where every new user lands): *"Put a crew on it."* — five agents take on your task while you watch. The "never ran" signal is **durable**: an `app_meta` marker stamped by `start_run` OR any surviving started row (`has_ever_started_run`) — it survives the monthly-counter reset AND the workspace-delete cascade that erases run rows. **CTA** checks readiness for **the flagship crew specifically** (Feature Factory is all-api on claude-* models → an *enabled Anthropic provider with a configured key*; a lone local provider would wave the user into a stage-1 failure): ready → hands off to the Direct launcher with **Feature Factory preselected** via a **workspace-scoped** `setLauncherPrefill` consumed **reactively** (the launcher is usually already mounted under the hidden overlay; a prefill addressed to another workspace stays parked — never leaks a brief across workspaces) and the workspace's task as the brief — one more click and the crew is working; not ready → opens **Settings · Models** with an honest toast and the invite survives. While shown, the invite runs the **readiness checks** once (shared `readinessStore`); when one fails (no `claude`, no `git`) it adds *"This Mac isn't ready for a crew yet."* with a serif **"See what's missing"** that opens Settings › General at the Readiness card. The click-time workspace is captured across the awaited check (a mid-await switch can't hijack the new workspace); an empty pipeline list is loaded on demand. "Not now" dismisses **persistently** (`octo-first-run` localStorage); the CTA hides it for the session; **a crew started via ANY path retires it immediately** (`noteRunStarted` from `runsStore.begin`/`start`). Beacon-legal (Talk has no brass live element; the CTA pulses). _Support:_ `src/components/FirstRunInvite.tsx`, `stores/firstRunStore.ts` (+ `crewProviderReady`), `App.handleSendFirstCrew`, `PipelineSetup` reactive prefill consume, command `has_ever_started_run` → `db.has_ever_started_run`/`mark_ever_ran`. _Entry:_ automatic, Talk canvas, first-ever session.
- **Empty-project state** — When a project has no active workspace: The Octo at 28px (`idle`, 80% opacity) above the eyebrow, then "No workspaces here yet… Create a workspace" CTA, overlaying only the canvas column (rail and status bar stay mounted/interactive, keeps PTYs alive). Gated on `workspacesByProjectId` (the rail's source of truth), not just `activeWorkspace` resolving to null — if the project actually has workspaces but `activeId` is stale, it self-heals (`healActiveForProject`) and activates one instead of ever showing the empty screen. When another project has workspaces loaded, an X icon ("Back to `<workspace>`" tooltip) plus Escape dismiss the screen and jump there, so it's never a dead end. _Support:_ `src/components/EmptyProjectState.tsx`; `src/App.tsx` (`hasStaleActiveState` gate, `dismissTarget`); `src/stores/workspaceStore.ts` (`healActiveForProject`). _Entry:_ open a project with zero workspaces.
- **Run empty state** — In Run mode with no terminals: "Start a new terminal.", the line "A terminal opens in the workspace's worktree directory. You can keep several sessions open, switch between them from the line above, or open them side by side." and the "Open terminal" CTA. _Support:_ `App.tsx` `RunEmptyState`. _Entry:_ Run mode, zero terminals.
- **Talk empty state — the Watcher** — The Octo at 72px whose eyes follow the mouse across the chat canvas (rAF lerp, ±2.4u, saturating at 240px); after 15s of keyboard silence it fidgets on a cycle — look around → scratch its head (back arm climbs the dome, eyes squint) → peek at the composer. Any keystroke re-arms the timer; reduced-motion renders the static idle pose. Above the `Talk` eyebrow, serif "Begin a conversation.", helper copy, then three upright-serif starters (`data-tour="talk-empty-starters"`): "Review what changed" (`@diff `), "Ask about a file" (`@`) and "Explain this workspace" ("Explain this workspace."). Each fills the composer after whatever is typed (`queueDraftInsert`, caret at the end, focus there) and sends nothing. _Support:_ `chat/OctoWatcher.tsx`; `ChatCanvas` `EmptyState`, `TALK_STARTERS`. _Entry:_ Talk mode, empty thread.
- **App icon & dev favicon** — The macOS/dock icon is The Octo (flat brass, back arms in muted brass, onyx rounded-rect field with the hairline atelier frame — no gradients) generated from `src-tauri/icons/source.svg` via `npm run tauri -- icon`; the Vite dev tab uses `public/favicon.svg` (mark only, back row omitted at favicon sizes). _Support:_ `src-tauri/icons/`; `index.html`. _Entry:_ dock, Finder, browser tab in dev.

### Toasts & notifications
- **Crew notifications (native)** — A macOS notification when a crew **needs a decision** or **finishes** — the first piece of "crews that work while you don't". Triggers map to the orchestrator's REAL signals: **needs-you ← `run://checkpoint` carrying `reason: "decision"`** (gate, halted stage, loop-at-cap, budget park; a Claude plan park that resumes on its own carries `reason: "plan_limit"` and gets a calm "Paused by your Claude plan" notice with `· resumes at 19:40` instead; the director's own "pause at the next stage" emits `reason: "director"` and stays **silent** — the user's own action is never a ping; a `paused` stage-update is NOT the signal: gates/halts never emit one); **finished ← stage-update transition to `completed`** (with the cost; `aborted` = the director's own hand). **Asymmetric focus policy:** needs-you fires **always** (`document.hasFocus()` stays true on a locked screen — a silent gate costs hours, a banner while watching costs nothing); finished stays quiet while focused (informative, not actionable). **No per-stage dedupe by design** — the orchestrator never re-emits for a still-parked stage, and a loop-back re-parking the same stage row genuinely needs a fresh ping. Bounded session maps; surrogate-safe body trims; `sendNotification` called directly (desktop permission is delivery-time on macOS — no stale grant cache). **A Talk approval card** waiting on you posts "Talk needs a decision" (`{workspace} — A command is waiting for your approval`, or `— A commit or push is waiting for your approval (possible secret)` for the secret guard's card: the kind of thing and the workspace, never the command or its arguments). Like a crew's needs-you ping it **always** fires: the app can't tell a locked screen from someone watching, and a banner while you watch costs nothing. Same toggle (`lib/approvalNotifications.ts`: pure `decideApprovalNotification` + `notifyApprovalWaiting`, called by `chatStore` on `chat://approval-request`). Toggle: Settings → General (default ON, persisted `octo-notify-prefs`). _Support:_ `src/lib/crewNotifications.ts` (pure `decideCheckpointNotification`/`decideCompletionNotification` + two listeners), `stores/notifyPrefsStore.ts`, `workspaceStore.findWorkspaceName` (shared with Mission Control), `tauri-plugin-notification` (+ capability). _Entry:_ automatic.
- **Notify me elsewhere (opt-in webhook, #964)** — One webhook URL the user sets in Settings › General › Attention gets a short JSON POST when a crew needs a decision while they are away from the Mac. It suits Slack-style and Discord-style incoming webhooks and any endpoint that accepts a JSON body; a service that shows whatever it receives (an ntfy topic URL, say) shows the raw JSON. **Off by default** (`notifyElsewhereEnabled`, `serde(default)` ⇒ `false` for every older `settings.json`). **Events and their fixed labels** (`notify_elsewhere::Event`, a closed set): `checkpoint_gate` "Checkpoint gate waiting" (a checkpoint gate, a gated or capped review loop, a budget park, a secret-guard hold), `director_question` "Question waiting for you" (`ask_director`), `plan_limit` "Claude plan limit, waiting for you" (a stage a Claude plan limit stopped, waiting for the director because its automatic resume is off, capped or used up, or the budget is spent; never reported as a failure, so a Routine that later resumes and finishes never sends "failed" first), `run_failed` "Crew run failed" (any other failed stage that halted the run), `routine_finished` "Routine finished" and `routine_failed` "Routine failed" (a Routine's run, told apart by `routines.last_run_id`, `db::routine_name_for_run`; a Routine's gate, question or plan limit is sent as `checkpoint_gate` / `director_question` / `plan_limit`), and `test`. A crew the director started finishing sends nothing, nor does the director's own pause (`reason: "director"`) or a Claude plan park that resumes on its own (`reason: "plan_limit"`); a Routine fire that skips its window (condition not met, busy, setup failed) sends nothing either. **The body** (`notify_elsewhere::payload`, the only builder; Rust tests pin the keys) has exactly five keys: `text` and `content` (the same string: Slack-style webhooks read `text`, Discord-style ones `content`), `mission`, `project` (the project's name) and `event` — e.g. `{"text":"Octopush · Checkpoint gate waiting · Add dark mode · acme-web","content":"…same…","mission":"Add dark mode","project":"acme-web","event":"checkpoint_gate"}`. `mission` is the workspace's mission title, which is the start of the mission's task as the user typed it (so it can read like a branch name); for a Routine's run it is the Routine's name (a fresh-mode Routine's workspace has no mission). Never code, diffs, the crew's questions or their recommended answers, stage artifacts, agent output, error messages, file paths, the repository URL, ids or costs. Names lose bidi controls and zero-width characters (U+202A–202E, U+2066–2069, U+200B–200F, U+2060, U+FEFF, U+061C) and other control characters, have whitespace collapsed, have `<` `>` `@` `[` `]` swapped for look-alikes (no `<!channel>`, `@everyone` or Markdown link can ride on a name) and are cut to 80 characters, so a body stays under 4 KB (`BODY_MAX_BYTES`) whatever the names hold; a usual one is a few hundred bytes. **Where it fires:** the orchestrator's existing attention points — `emit_checkpoint` (the same `run://checkpoint` choke point the native ping and the Dock badge read) and the run's completion in `drive_inner` (`orchestrator/notify.rs`). Both run in the app's own drive **and in `octopush-run-worker`**, which drives with the same orchestrator, so a detached crew (and every Routine run) reaches the webhook with the app closed; the worker waits for in-flight sends (`notify_elsewhere::flush`, at most 15 s) before it exits. The detached bridge relays a worker's park to the window with `relay_checkpoint` and never sends it again. It does send the parks the worker could not (a worker that died, or exited without settling), but only while the app is open: the bridge runs in the app, so a worker that dies with the app closed is sent nothing until the app opens and repairs the run. **The sender** (`notify_elsewhere.rs`): `https` only, or `http` to this Mac (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`) for a local test receiver; no user name or password in the URL; ≤ 2048 characters (`validate_url`, enforced when saving, so an invalid URL is never stored). The hardened TLS client (`tls::client_builder`) with a 3 s connect and 5 s total timeout, **no redirects followed** (a 3xx is a failure), user agent `Octopush`; spawned, so a run never waits; at most **one retry** (2 s later, only for a network error, a timeout, 429 or 5xx), so delivery is **at least once**: a retry after a timeout can deliver a message twice if the first attempt did arrive. The setting is re-read before every attempt, so turning it off (or changing the URL) stops even a pending retry. The URL is never logged or written to a journal (webhook URLs carry their secret). A failed send is **one quiet notice** in the parked stage's journal — "Notify me elsewhere didn't send: the webhook answered HTTP 404." — and a `tracing` warning with the event kind and the cause; the run is never affected. **Settings UI** (`NotifyElsewhereRow`, `data-tour="settings-notify-elsewhere"`): label, helper text ("… It carries a fixed label, the project's name and the mission's title (the start of its task), never code, diffs, questions or agent output. Off until you turn it on; Send a test posts one test message either way."), switch (`notify-elsewhere-switch`, disabled with the tooltip "Add a webhook URL first" until the field has one; a click shows at once and the backend's answer settles it, a refused save puts it back), the URL field (`settings-notify-elsewhere-url`; mono, serif placeholder `https://hooks.example.com/…`, saved on blur or Enter through `set_notify_elsewhere`; saves run one after another, so typing a URL and clicking the switch turns it on in one click; clearing the field turns the setting off; the backend's refusal shows in rouge under it and the saved state stays), **"Send a test"** (`settings-notify-elsewhere-test`; posts the `test` body with the example names to the URL in the field, saved or not, on or off, once with no retry; "Sending…" while in flight, then "Test sent. The webhook accepted it." or "The test didn't send: <cause>."). One status line under the field ("Saved", the test result or the refusal) grows and folds on the grid-rows `Reveal` and crossfades between messages (`FadeSwap`). A folded **"The message's fields"** disclosure (`settings-notify-elsewhere-payload`, grid-rows `Reveal`) shows the fields of the body for a checkpoint gate with the example names "Example mission" / "Example project", straight from the backend (`notify_elsewhere_preview`) and pretty-printed (the wire form is compact), and every `event` value. Free and Pro alike. _Support:_ `src-tauri/src/notify_elsewhere.rs`, `orchestrator/notify.rs`, `orchestrator/mod.rs` (`emit_checkpoint` / `relay_checkpoint`, completion), `orchestrator/bridge.rs`, `bin/octopush-run-worker/main.rs` (flush), `settings.rs` (`notifyElsewhereEnabled` / `notifyElsewhereUrl`, `set_notify_elsewhere`, carried over by whole-file saves), `db.rs` (`routine_name_for_run`), commands `get_notify_elsewhere` / `set_notify_elsewhere` / `notify_elsewhere_test` / `notify_elsewhere_preview`; `src/components/settings/NotifyElsewhereRow.tsx`. _Entry:_ Settings › General › Attention.
- **Detached runs (crews survive quitting) — Pro** — Every Direct run a Pro user starts, resumes (checkpoint approve/reject/resume), or re-runs executes in a **detached segment worker** (`octopush-run-worker`, a sidecar like the PTY daemon): the app reserves a cross-process **worker lease** on the `runs` row (`worker_nonce`/`worker_pid`/`heartbeat_at`), spawns the worker in its own session (`setsid`), and the worker drives ONE segment (start → next pause/completion) with the same `Orchestrator` — so **quitting Octopush no longer kills in-flight crews**; the `claude` CLI child lives in the worker's session and survives too. The **detached bridge** (app-side ~1.2s tick) re-emits the worker's persisted progress as the same `run://stage-update`/`run://cost`/`run://log`/`run://checkpoint`/`run://context` events, so Mission Control, the live journal, and crew notifications work unchanged; it **adopts** leases from a previous app session (replaying the running stage's current attempt into the live pane, capped at 200 rows) and **repairs** runs whose worker died while the app is open (`reconcile_stale_leases`: a heartbeat older than 45s → the standard interrupted/Resume flow + a needs-you ping). A worker that died while the app was closed is repaired at the next launch by startup recovery (`recover_interrupted_runs`) into the same Resume shape but **without a ping**: the run just waits under Needs you in Mission Control. Controls route cross-process: stop-stage/pause write `stop_requested`/`pause_requested` flags the worker polls (~1s); abort needs nothing new (the status write is already durable); the director's own pause keeps `reason: "director"` (no false ping). Startup recovery (`recover_interrupted_runs`) **skips fresh-leased runs** — the one change that lets a live worker coexist with an app relaunch. A segment that parks at a Claude plan limit with an automatic resume scheduled keeps the worker waiting for the reset, then it resumes the run itself (see Halt detection › "Claude plan limit park"). If the segment ends while the app is closed, the worker posts a **native notification** via `osascript` ("Crew finished" / "The crew needs you"); aborts stay silent. With "Notify me elsewhere" on, the worker also posts the park or the Routine's end to the webhook itself and waits for that send before it exits, whether or not the app is open (the bridge only relays it; see "Notify me elsewhere"). The worker never migrates the DB (`Db::open_without_migrations`), never reads the keychain, never syncs history (`Orchestrator::new_headless`; the bridge syncs on its behalf). Any spawn failure falls back to the in-process drive — detachment never costs a run. Free stays fully in-process — but is **no longer silent about it**: the Direct launcher's unattended-readiness affordance surfaces a locked `Unattended · Pro` chip → `runs.detached` upsell (see "Unattended readiness"), so detachment is a discoverable Pro capability rather than an invisible fallback. Mission Control cards show a quiet `Moon` icon on running detached runs ("Working detached — this crew keeps going even if you quit Octopush"). _Support:_ `src-tauri/src/bin/octopush-run-worker/main.rs`, `orchestrator/worker.rs` (spawn + lease reserve), `orchestrator/bridge.rs` (watch/replay/repair), `db.rs` lease + control-flag helpers + `repair_interrupted_run`/`reconcile_stale_leases`, `entitlement::feature::RUNS_DETACHED`, routing in `commands::{start_run, resolve_checkpoint, rerun_from_stage, stop_stage, request_run_pause}`; design record `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-12-detached-runs-phase1-design.md`. _Entry:_ automatic for Pro.
- **Routines (scheduled crews) — Pro** — A saved pipeline that fires on a **schedule** and drives itself, closing the "crews that work while you don't" pillar: set it once and a review runs every morning or a dependency sweep every few hours, each fire executing as a **detached** run (so it survives the app quitting once started). An in-app **scheduler** (`routines::spawn_routine_scheduler`, a 30s tokio tick beside the detached bridge) selects enabled routines whose `next_due_at` has passed and fires each through the **exact same guarded launch** a user's Begin uses — the guard sequence (same-workspace concurrency, worker lease, monthly quota, parallel-runs gate, budget, first-run marker, detached-spawn + in-process fallback) was extracted into one shared `orchestrator::launch::launch_run` so `commands::start_run` and the scheduler can never drift. Phase 1 fires only while the app runs; a window missed while closed **catches up once** on the next tick (`next_due` jumps to the next future slot — never N times). **Schedule kinds:** `interval` (every N minutes/hours), `daily` (at HH:MM machine-local), and **`recurring`** — the flexible **Days × Times** model whose `schedule_spec` is a JSON string `{days, time}` (no DB migration): **days** = `{kind:"weekly", set:[…ISO 1=Mon…7=Sun]}` (covers every-day, weekdays, or any subset) or `{kind:"date", date:"YYYY-MM-DD"}` (a one-shot); **time** = `{kind:"once", at:"HH:MM"}` or `{kind:"window", start, everyMinutes, end}` (fires `start, start+every, … ≤ end`; `everyMinutes ≥ 15`). So "Mon/Wed/Fri at 9am", "one specific date", and "every hour 9am–3pm" are all one control. The **entire scheduler rests on the one pure `next_due(kind, spec, after)`** — the tick, catch-up, fixed/fresh, and the fire-condition gate only call it — so `recurring` is contained behind `next_due` + `validate_schedule` (scans forward ≤400 days for the next active-day fire; DST-safe via `local_at`; a past one-shot → None). A `next_n_due` helper backs the editor's live **`preview_routine_schedule`** command (the "next runs" list uses the *real* engine — no second implementation). `next_due` is a pure, unit-tested computation stored in **UTC** so the SQL due-comparison is valid across DST. **Workspace modes:** `fixed` (run in a chosen workspace; a fire is skipped while a previous run is active — `workspace_has_active_run`) and `fresh` (a new worktree on a unique timestamped branch each fire — the isolated "ship a change every day" mode; a runaway guard skips while the routine's own previous run is still active, and phase 1 requires `fresh` to fire **at most once a day** — `validate_routine` now takes the spec: `daily`, or `recurring` with a single `once` time, is allowed; `interval` and a `recurring` `window` are rejected — because there's no auto-reaper yet, so one worktree/day is the bound; the git checkout runs on `spawn_blocking`). A `fresh` worktree then runs the project's **setup-script template** (`projects.setup_script`, the wizard's last-used script) headless before the crew — `bash -c` in the worktree with the login-shell PATH and Conductor's `CONDUCTOR_*` variables (see Workspaces › Conductor variables), bounded by a 10-minute timeout (`routines::run_setup`); a failure discards the worktree (and the branch it created) only when this fire created it (`CreateOutcome::Created`, `routines::discards_on_setup_failure` — an adopted or reused checkout is never wiped), creates no run and skips with `setup failed: exit N · <stderr tail>` (`SkipReason::SetupFailed`). **Claude plan wall:** before anything else (no condition, worktree, setup script, run or tokens), a fire whose crew — the Routine's own model overrides applied — has a Claude Code CLI stage skips while the stored Claude plan snapshot has a window `rejected` (not covered by extra usage) with a future reset that applies to one of its Claude Code stages: `plan limit · resets 19:40` (`SkipReason::PlanLimit { resets_at }`, token `plan_limit`, the latest such reset; `routines::plan_wall`, pure). The 5-hour and weekly windows apply to every model; a model's own window (`seven_day_opus`) only to a stage on that model, so a rejected Opus week never skips a Sonnet crew. A snapshot seen more than 6 hours ago (`PLAN_WALL_MAX_AGE_SECS`, `fresh_plan_windows`) no longer skips: the wall may have lifted, and a fire that meets it parks and refreshes the snapshot. API and Codex crews never skip on it. **The two setup paths use different shells:** a mission's setup terminal runs the script under the user's `$SHELL -l -c` (zsh by default, with its rc files), while a Routine runs it under `bash -c` with the login-shell PATH — so zsh-only syntax or aliases work in the wizard's terminal but not in a Routine's fresh worktree; keep a script meant for Routines POSIX/bash. A condition or setup script still running when the app quits is killed with its whole process group (`routines::kill_live_groups` on `RunEvent::Exit`; a dropped fire kills its group too, via `GroupGuard`), as the timeout path does. The scheduler advances `next_due` BEFORE any side effect so a crash can't double-fire; a run refused at launch is deleted (not aborted, which would pollute the monthly meter). The scheduler re-checks the `routines.scheduled` entitlement before every fire (a downgrade silently stops firing) and never kills its loop on a per-routine failure. The double-fire guard is the `next_due` advance written **before** any side effect; `last_fired_at`/`last_run_id` are stamped after the run is created. A fixed routine whose target workspace was deleted auto-disables (rather than skipping every window forever). **Optional pre-fire condition (`fire_condition`):** a routine may carry an optional shell command evaluated before each fire — **exit 0 ⇒ fire, exit 1 ⇒ skip** the window with **no run created and zero tokens** (and for `fresh` mode, **no throwaway worktree** — the gate runs BEFORE the workspace is resolved/created, right after the busy check and after the crash-safe `next_due` advance). It's fully **generic** (any command, any pipeline): e.g. a routine that addresses new PR-review comments hourly skips the idle windows with `gh pr view --json reviewThreads -q '…' | grep -q .`. The command runs under `bash -c` with the **user's login-shell PATH**: a GUI app starts from launchd's minimal `/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`, and `bash -l` never reads zsh's rc files, so `routines::condition_path` asks the user's `$SHELL -l -i -c` for its `$PATH` (read between markers so rc-file output is ignored; `~/.zprofile` *and* `~/.zshrc`, where Homebrew, nvm and `~/.local/bin` land) **once per app session, cached, with a 5s timeout** (`login_shell_path`; a slow or interactive rc file falls back to the inherited PATH instead of hanging a routine), merged ahead of the inherited PATH — so `gh`, `node`, `npx` and `claude` resolve. Same trust model as a run's `run_command`/setup scripts (their command, their machine) — with **cwd = the routine's workspace** (fixed mode → the fixed workspace's `worktree_path`; fresh mode → the project root, since the fresh worktree doesn't exist yet) and a **30s timeout** (`tokio::time::timeout`, the child killed on timeout) so a hung check can never stall the 30s scheduler tick. A spawn failure, a timeout, or **any exit other than 0 or 1** (`classify_condition_exit` — e.g. exit 2 from a script's own error path, 127 for a missing program) is a **fail-safe skip** (never a blind fire) recorded as **"condition error: exit N · <last 2 stderr lines>"** (`stderr_tail`, capped at 160 chars), so a broken check (`condition error: exit 127 · bash: gh: command not found`) never looks like a legitimate "condition not met". **Legibility (`last_checked_at`/`last_outcome`):** every evaluation — dispatch or skip — stamps the outcome ("dispatched" / "condition not met" / "condition error: …" / "workspace busy" / "workspace unavailable") and a timestamp, so a routine that keeps skipping stays legible in the list ("condition not met · 2m ago") instead of looking dead. **UI:** a **Settings → Routines** pane (new `Automation` group) — declarative, zero new top-level chrome (Atelier-compliant): a routine list (name · schedule · project · workspace mode · `conditional` marker · next-fire · last-outcome/checked-ago · pause toggle · run-now · edit · delete) + a `ModalShell` editor (project → pipeline → schedule → workspace mode → brief → optional **"Fire only if…"** mono command field with an exit-0 explainer → optional budget; the project/pipeline/workspace pickers are keyboard-navigable Atelier `Listbox`es, not native `<select>`s). The schedule control is Daily / Every / **Custom** — Custom reveals the **Days × Times builder** (`RecurringBuilder`): preset chips (Every day · Weekdays · Days of week · Time window · On a date) → day-of-week chips (or a date field) × a Once/Window time mode, with an always-visible **live natural-language summary** and a **"Next runs" preview** (via `preview_routine_schedule` — the real engine, debounced). Fresh mode offers only single-time schedules (the ≤1/day rule). A non-Pro user sees an upgrade banner (its CTA is the ceremonial brass-ghost serif phrase "Put your crews on a schedule with Pro", `data-tour="routines-upsell-cta"`, which opens the checkout) but can still see and delete/pause routines they authored while Pro. `run_routine_now` fires immediately through the **identical** fire path — the condition gate included — and reports honestly whether a run was dispatched or the window was skipped **and why** (`{ outcome, reason?, skip? }`, `skip` = `SkipReason::token`), so "Run now" is an honest test of exactly what a scheduled fire would do; to force a fire regardless, the user clears the condition. While it is in flight the row shows what it is waiting on — `checking its condition…` · `making a fresh workspace…` · `running the setup script…` · `launching the crew…` (`data-tour="routines-run-now-phase"`, also the run-now button's tooltip) — from the `routine://phase` events every fire emits (`{ routineId, phase }`, `routines::PHASE_*`; `routinesStore.phaseById`, `describeRoutinePhase`). A Routine whose crew, with the Routine's own model overrides, uses a model that retires within 30 days shows one amber mono line under its row: "Sonnet 4.5 retires Nov 30, so this routine will fail from then on." After the date the line turns rouge: "…retired Nov 30, so this routine will fail." The tooltip names only the fix the app offers for how that Routine reaches the model (`modelRetirement.routineRetirementFix`): a Routine that inherits a custom crew's model is fixed by switching that crew from the Direct launcher; a Routine on a builtin crew isn't, because the switch saves a copy, "<name> (custom)", and the Routine keeps the builtin until it's edited to use the copy; and a Routine whose own stage overrides pick the model (set through MCP `create_routine`) isn't either, because the launcher switch edits only the crew's stages and the routine editor doesn't show overrides, so the tooltip says to compose it again (a new routine has none) and delete the old one (`modelRetirement.routineRetirement`; the first such row carries `data-tour="routines-model-retirement"`; see Direct "Retiring model"). A setup failure gets its own **Setup failed** error toast (with the exit and stderr tail) instead of the "Nothing to run" skip toast. Commands: `list_routines`/`create_routine`/`update_routine`/`delete_routine` (deletion ungated) `/set_routine_enabled`/`run_routine_now` (all but delete Pro-gated via `require_feature_gate`), plus `preview_routine_schedule` (read-only, ungated — the editor's next-runs preview). **Secret guard:** a Routine-fired run whose Action stage (pull request, merge, release) finds a possible secret in the worktree — or can't check it in full — parks needs-you like any Direct run and never opens the PR on its own (see §4 "Secret guard hold"). **Notify me elsewhere:** with it on, a Routine's run that completes sends `routine_finished` and one that fails sends `routine_failed`, both with the Routine's name as `mission`; its gates, questions and plan limits send like any crew's (a plan limit never as "failed") (see §Toasts "Notify me elsewhere"). _Support:_ `src-tauri/src/routines.rs` (scheduler + pure `next_due`/`validate_schedule`/`validate_routine` + the `recurring` types `RecurringSpec`/`DaySel`/`TimeSel` + `next_due_recurring`/`next_n_due` + `evaluate_condition`/`FireOutcome`/`SkipReason`), `orchestrator/launch.rs` (shared guarded launch), `db.rs` `routines` table (`fire_condition`/`last_checked_at`/`last_outcome` columns) + CRUD (`insert_routine`/`list_due_routines`/`mark_routine_fired`/`set_routine_fire_result`/`workspace_has_active_run`), `entitlement::feature::ROUTINES_SCHEDULED`, `commands::{list,create,update,delete,set_enabled,run_now}_routine`; frontend `src/components/settings/RoutinesPane.tsx`, `lib/routineForm.ts` (pure form logic), `stores/routinesStore.ts`, `lib/settingsTabs.ts` (`Automation` group); design records `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-13-routines-phase1-design.md` + `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-15-routine-fire-condition-design.md` + `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-31-routine-recurring-schedule-design.md`. _Entry:_ Settings → Routines.
- **Dock badge** — The Dock icon shows how many runs need you (the fleet chip's count) plus the Talk conversations whose approval card waits on you, cleared at 0, and keeps counting while the window is closed (on macOS, closing it hides it; the app keeps running until ⌘Q). See §10 "OS-integration". _Support:_ `src-tauri/src/fleet_status.rs`. _Entry:_ automatic.
- **Menu bar Octo (#718)** — On macOS, The Octo sits in the menu bar with the needs-you count beside it (only above 0), and its menu lists the crews that need you and the Talk conversations whose approval card waits, longest-waiting first; choosing one opens that crew, or that conversation in Talk. On by default; Settings › General › Attention › "Show in menu bar". See §10 "OS-integration". _Support:_ `src-tauri/src/menu_bar.rs`. _Entry:_ the menu bar.
- **Toast system** — Bottom-right stacked toasts (info/success/warning/error), auto-dismiss after `timeout` (default 5000ms) or manual `X`; imperative global `pushToast(...)`. _Support:_ `src/components/Toasts.tsx`. _Entry:_ programmatic across the app.
- **Backend-event toasts** — Listens for `octopush://budget-warning`, `octopush://session-error`, `pty://exit` and raises matching toasts. _Support:_ `Toasts.tsx`.
- **Startup "restored sessions" toast** — Fires once if any terminals were restored. _Support:_ `App.tsx`.
- **Budget-threshold toasts** — On chat-stream completion, fires 50% (info) / 80% (warning) / 100% (error, "Budget cap hit — Send blocked") toasts once per threshold per scope. _Support:_ `App.tsx`; `budgetsStore.notifiedThresholds`.
- **Attention chime** — Background chat/terminal completions ring a synthesized two-note brass chime (~250ms), rate-limited to one per 2s, with an AudioContext autoplay-unlock on first gesture; toggle in Settings → General. _Support:_ `src/stores/attentionStore.ts`. _Entry:_ automatic.
- **UpdateNotifier** — Corner update toast mounted at the shell root (see §10). _Support:_ `App.tsx` `<UpdateNotifier />`.
- **What's new dialog (post-update tips)** — After an update, a `ModalShell` dialog shows one tip per page for every version in (last seen, installed]: eyebrow *What's new* + version span, serif title, inline-Markdown body (bold, code, links open in the browser), an optional muted looping clip (`<slug>.webm`; under reduced motion no autoplay, a Play/Pause control instead), `StageDots` page position (`tone="pager"`: seen pages verdigris, the current page the one brass dot, upcoming hairline), **Back** / **Next** (←/→) / **Done**, and **Show me** when the tip has tour steps — the dialog steps aside, the guided tour runs, then it returns at the next tip. Tips are the `area: app` changesets with `highlight` (default on for feature/improvement, off for fix), bundled at build time via `import.meta.glob` over the released `whats-new/X.Y.Z/` dirs (`unreleased/` never ships). `lastSeenVersion` persists in localStorage (`octo-whats-new`); a fresh install records it silently, while an existing install without the key (upgrading to the first version that records it — detected from other persisted prefs) sees the installed version's tips; an upgrade with no tips stays silent; the dialog waits until no other dialog, update alert or tour holds the screen and only then marks the version seen (if the user opens it by hand meanwhile, that counts and the wait ends). After **Show me**, everything the tour opened (Settings, palette, Mission Control, Logbook) closes again (`octo:navigate` `close-overlays`). Reopen via the palette (**What's new**) or Settings › About (**What's in this version**). _Support:_ `src/lib/whatsNew.ts` (parse/group/semver/launch decision), `src/lib/whatsNewBundle.ts`, `src/lib/whatsNewLaunch.ts`, `src/stores/whatsNewStore.ts`, `src/components/WhatsNewModal.tsx`, `WhatsNewHost.tsx` (mounted in both the welcome and workspace shells). _Entry:_ automatic after an update; ⌘K → What's new; Settings › About.
- **Guided tour (Show me)** — Walks a changeset's `steps` over the real UI: opens the step's named surface (`src/lib/tour/surfaces.ts`), waits ≤ 2s for a visible `[data-tour]` target (MutationObserver + rAF), else skips the step; a scrim with a cut-out and a hairline brass outline follows the target, a caption bubble anchors to it (flips at viewport edges); Back / Next / Done, ←/→, Escape closes, focus trapped and restored, clicks on the app are blocked. The interactive tour never performs actions. `data-tour` anchors are listed in `docs/WHATS-NEW.md` §2. _Support:_ `src/lib/tour/runner.ts`, `src/stores/tourStore.ts`, `src/components/TourOverlay.tsx`, `.octo-tour-spot`. _Entry:_ What's new → Show me.
- **Clip-recorder bridge (`window.__octoTour`)** — `play(steps, { mode: "interactive" | "record", stepMs? })`; record mode auto-advances every `stepMs` (2200 default) and performs each step's `action` (click / hover / type). Installed only in dev builds or with `?octo-record=1`. _Support:_ `src/lib/tour/bridge.ts`. _Entry:_ the clip recorder.
- **Dev: Preview unreleased tips** — Dev-build-only palette action that opens the dialog with `whats-new/unreleased/` tips. _Support:_ `CommandPalette.tsx`, `whatsNewLaunch.ts` `previewUnreleasedTips`.

### Cross-cutting overlays, menus & dialogs
- **ModalShell** — Canonical dialog chrome: portal-to-body, tokenized scrim, `.octo-overlay-enter` + `.octo-modal-enter`, Escape (topmost-only via an `escStack`), focus-in/restore (an optional `initialFocus` ref takes focus on open, and again a frame later if focus was left on the dialog itself or on nothing), Tab trap, optional click-outside, center/top alignment; exposes `isModalOpen()`. **Focus is restored with `preventScroll`** — handing focus back scrolls the opener into view, and the editor's `.cm-content` is one contenteditable spanning the whole document, so its "into view" is its top: without this, closing *any* dialog opened from the editor threw the reader back to line 1 of the file they were reading. _Support:_ `src/components/ModalShell.tsx`. _Entry:_ reused by palettes, dialogs, modals.
- **MenuSurface** — Canonical context-menu chrome: portal-to-body, `.octo-menu-enter`, viewport clamping + arrow-key nav + Escape/outside-click via `useMenuChrome`. Rows use `MENU_ITEM` / `MENU_ITEM_MULTILINE` (`src/lib/menuStyles.ts`), whose keyboard focus wears the hover's brass-ghost wash and brass text (`focus-visible:`), never the browser's focus ring. _Support:_ `src/components/MenuSurface.tsx`. _Entry:_ underlies all context menus.
- **Workspace / Project / Backlog context menus** — Right-click a rail monogram, project header, or Jira ticket — see §2 and §9 for full item lists. _Support:_ `App.tsx`; `WorkspaceContextMenu`, `ProjectContextMenu`, `BacklogRowContextMenu`.
- **Settings overlay** — Full Settings opened to a specific tab; refreshes the issue-tracker-configured flag on save. _Support:_ `App.tsx`; `Settings`. _Entry:_ ⌘, / ⌘⇧T / top bar / palette.

### Motion & UI primitives
- **FadeSwap** — Crossfades mutually-exclusive views by key (outgoing `.octo-fade-out` 120ms, then `.octo-fade-in`); honors reduced-motion. _Support:_ `src/components/primitives/FadeSwap.tsx`.
- **Reveal** — Mounted expand/collapse via grid-rows `0fr↔1fr` + opacity; closed content is `inert`. _Support:_ `src/components/primitives/Reveal.tsx`.
- **prefersReducedMotion()** — Shared JS guard for reduced-motion. _Support:_ `src/lib/motion.ts`.

### Notable implementation details
- `activeMode` is derived from `modePerWorkspace[activeWorkspaceId] || "talk"`. All four mode canvases stay mounted as opacity-gated `ModeOverlay`s (no unmount on switch). A single `window` `keydown` listener (`src/hooks/useGlobalShortcuts.ts`, called from `App.tsx`) owns every global shortcut (see Appendix C).
- **Attention model** — `attentionStore.ping(wsId, kind, terminalId?, reason?)` flags a workspace ("chat"→Talk, "terminal"→Run) and chimes; App mirrors `{workspaceId, mode}` into `src/lib/focus.ts` and clears a flag only when the user is on the matching mode of the flagged workspace. **A Talk approval card is a state, not a ping:** `raiseApproval(wsId, command, chime)` raises a chat flag with `reason: "approval"` and the oldest card still waiting as `detail` (it follows the cards as they are answered, while `since` and `at` stay at the first card, so the beacon can't hop), no focus clears it (`shouldClearAttention` → false, `isApprovalFlag`), no later ping replaces it (a terminal ping still records its session's wait), and `settleApproval(wsId)` drops it, and only it, once the workspace's last card is answered. `chatStore` keeps the two in step from one place: a store subscription on `pendingApprovalsByWs` raises the flag while any card waits and settles it when none does, whatever removed the card (a click, Stop, a deleted conversation, `approval-resolved`, a reload's rehydrate).
- **PTY survival architecture** — `allTerminalRefs` flattens `terminalsByWs` so every `TerminalPane` mounts at once (only the active one visible), keeping PTYs + scrollback alive across project switches. The panes live in one always-mounted `TerminalHost` (`src/components/TerminalHost.tsx`), a sibling of the mode overlays: the Run canvas renders a `TerminalSlot` placeholder that measures itself (ResizeObserver) and publishes its rect to `terminalSlotsStore`, and the host draws each pane in a frame over its slot in the active mode only (hidden overlays still measure; a pane with no slot there stays `display:none`). Frames are keyed by session and never re-parented, so switching sessions or modes never remounts or replays a pane; the host layer fades in with the overlays' own opacity transition (leaving Run hides the frames at once, as before) and the frame origin lives in the same store so a pane never lags its slot while the canvas moves; the layer passes the pointer through except over a placed pane. The host holds the Run `panel` error boundary inside that layer, so its card shows only in Run. Only the card takes the pointer (`interactive`); the full-size fallback around it stays pointer-transparent, so the pane captions around it keep working; **Try again** remounts the panes, which reattach to their daemon PTYs. A module-level `terminalInitInFlight` Set guards against double-creation of the auto-"Main" terminal.
- **Git/PR refresh cadence** — Git status refreshes on workspace/mode change, on window focus, and on a 3s interval only in run/review (skipped while hidden); the diff is built only in Review. On window focus the app also **refreshes every externally-authored surface** — `octopush-mcp` is a separate process writing to the same SQLite store and cannot emit Tauri events, so on return from another app it re-lists **workspaces** (`loadAllWorkspaces` — rail), **pipelines** (`pipelineStore.load` — the ensemble picker), and the **active workspace's runs** (`runsStore.loadRuns` — incl. MCP-staged drafts). Background refetches never clobber UI state: `loadRuns(…, { background: true })` is **sticky-active** — the viewed canvas is never reassigned under the user (a newly staged draft surfaces in the RUNS list, never by stealing the launcher/view; only a vanished/terminal active is replaced, and then only by an *executing* run), the launcher repairs its pipeline selection against the new list and **resets position-keyed model overrides if the selected pipeline was restructured externally** (they would otherwise retarget onto the wrong stage), and run rows are keyed by id; no new timers. Open-PR is fetched per workspace-switch then every 60s. Token usage refreshes every 30s and on chat-turn completion.

## 2. Projects, Missions & Workspaces

Missions are the **first-level unit of intent** (build/fix/review/probe/design/perf/ops/test). A *code* mission (build/fix) owns exactly one **workspace**, and workspaces **are git worktrees** living as siblings of the project root under `<parent>/.octopus-worktrees/<branch>/`. The **main workspace** is special: its `worktree_path` equals the project root (git forbids the default branch checked out twice), so the project root *is* the main worktree. Isolation is a property a mission chooses along two axes — git-state (`worktree`/`readonly`/`ephemeral`/`pr`) and execution (`none`/`sandbox`/`container`/`cloud`).

### Missions (threads of intent)
- **Missions as the first-level unit** — Every workspace is born paired with a `build` mission; the pairing is idempotent, so a reused/adopted workspace keeps its mission and no workspace ever exists without one. (Design/probe missions arriving with later movements may have no worktree.) The active mission's intent surfaces as a glyph + label eyebrow above the workspace name in the ContextHeader. A partial unique index guarantees the core invariant: **never two active missions writing one checkout** — readonly missions may share a checkout freely, but their agent context is always their own. **Intent × git state (#1239):** `build`/`fix`/`design`/`ops` *deliver* (`mission::delivers`) and take any git state; `review`/`probe`/`perf` take `readonly` or `ephemeral`; `test` takes only `ephemeral`. A new mission that pairs a non-delivering intent with `worktree` or `pr`, or `test` with anything but `ephemeral`, is refused with an error naming the intent (`mission::validate_axes`, IPC and MCP alike); stored rows keep loading. A non-delivering mission that isn't `readonly` **ships nothing** (`mission::ships_nothing`, derived, never stored), so an older `review` + `worktree` row now reads as ship-nothing, which only narrows it. _Support:_ `missions` table + nullable `mission_id` back-refs on `runs`/`chat_threads`/`terminals` (`src-tauri/src/db.rs`); the shared `src-tauri/src/mission.rs` (`create` / `ensure_for_workspace`, one code path also used by `octopush-mcp`); commands `create_mission` / `list_missions` / `get_mission` / `update_mission` / `archive_mission`; `src/stores/missionsStore.ts`; the `ContextHeader` intent chip (`INTENT_ICON`). A one-shot, `app_meta`-gated backfill re-parents every existing workspace into a `build` mission on upgrade. _Entry:_ automatic on workspace creation; intent chip in the header.
- **Sandboxed execution (macOS seatbelt) — free** — A mission's second isolation axis, `exec_isolation`, becomes real: with `exec_isolation = "sandbox"`, the mission's agents run **write-confined to the workspace**. The guarantee: an agent **cannot modify files outside its own mission** (other worktrees, `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.config`, `~/Documents`, system paths all stay read-only); **network stays open**, and so does any read Claude Code's permission checker can't see (a script or build tool opening a file itself). **Claude Code's file tools can't read outside the worktree either:** in a mission whose own `exec_isolation` is `sandbox`, the Claude CLI stages (fresh and resumed) get `"blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories":true` in their `--settings` beside the write guard, so Read/Grep/Glob refuse `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws` or a sibling repo (Claude Code ≥ 2.1.257; on an older known CLI the launch line says `file reads not confined (Claude Code 2.1.257+ needed)`; see CLI substrate). Each sandboxed Claude stage gets its own temp dir, `~/Library/Caches/octopush/tmp/<key>` (0700, one per build-cache root, so only Claude stages of the same workspace, access mode, exec choice and read guard share it), and `TMPDIR` points there instead of the user-wide `$TMPDIR`. With the read guard on, that temp dir and the build-cache root are the only dirs passed with `--add-dir`, so the stage can still read its own temp files and the caches its builds write. The user-wide `$TMPDIR` is never added: every app, workspace and stage writes there, and Claude Code loads `.claude/skills`, agents and commands from an `--add-dir` dir, so it would let any process plant skills in the stage. A tool that ignores `TMPDIR` and writes `/tmp` directly still can (it stays writable), but the stage's file tools can't read that back. A review/probe (`readonly`) mission whose exec choice is `none` is still sandboxed (forced on, temp-only writes) but does **not** get the read guard: the guard follows the user's own choice (`StageContext.exec_choice`), not the forced-on tier. The setting reaches Bash too: a shell command that Claude Code's checker sees reading outside the working directories (`cat ~/.ssh/…`, `cd .. && git log`) asks for permission, and a headless stage has nobody to answer, so it is refused. A read the checker can't see still succeeds, because the Seatbelt profile denies writes only. The shell is narrowed, not closed. **Claude Code's own Bash sandbox is off inside the profile (#1001):** every Claude stage the profile wraps (a sandboxed mission, and a readonly one whose sandbox is forced on; fresh and resumed) also gets `"sandbox":{"enabled":false}` in its `--settings` beside the guards (`cli_runner::turn_off_inner_sandbox`). A Bash sandbox the user turned on in `~/.claude/settings.json` can't nest in the profile, and since Claude Code 2.1.328 the next sandboxed Bash command would then be refused. The launch line says `Claude Code's own Bash sandbox is off here: Octopush's sandbox confines this stage`. If Claude Code still refuses a Bash command with "the sandbox is off for the session" in a stage the profile wraps (say, a managed policy forces the sandbox on), the done card's last line says it refused a Bash command (`cli_runner::INNER_SANDBOX_OFF`). Only an error result of a `Bash` call counts (`cli_runner::InnerSandboxWatch`), so a Read, Grep or `cat` of a file quoting the phrase doesn't, and unsandboxed stages aren't watched. When that refusal is the stage's last Bash result and the stage failed, its halt names it too and the stage isn't escalated, since a stronger model meets the same refusal; when a later Bash command ran, the failure keeps its own error and escalates as usual. Confinement covers **every execution surface**: (1) the **CLI substrate** (`sandbox-exec -p <profile> claude …`) — enforced at the single spawn in `orchestrator/cli_runner.rs`, so the in-process orchestrator **and** the detached/unattended worker are covered identically (both use `CliRunner`; `exec_isolation` re-derived per stage, no cross-process state); (2) **in-process tool execution** — TALK's inline tools and API-substrate DIRECT stages call `chat_engine::execute_tool`, which for a sandboxed mission runs BOTH `run_command` and `write_file` through the **kernel-enforced** seatbelt: `run_command` wraps its shell (with the login-shell PATH, set after the cache redirections; see Talk "Login-shell PATH for every Talk shell"), and `write_file` writes via a seatbelt-wrapped `mkdir -p … && cat > "$1"` (target passed as a positional arg, content piped on stdin) so the **kernel resolves symlinks** — a lexical check can't see through a committed `link -> $HOME`, so the write is done under the sandbox, not trusted to a string check (`sandbox::is_write_allowed` remains only a cheap pre-filter). A sandboxed TALK turn routes `run_command` away from the shared shell to the per-command sandboxed path. **No silent fallback:** if the sandbox can't be set up (non-macOS, missing driver, a build-cache root that can't be created) — or the mission asks for a not-yet-implemented tier (`container`/`cloud`) — the work **fails with a readable error** rather than running unconfined; security never degrades quietly. The profile is `(allow default)` → `(deny file-write*)` → re-allow writes under the workspace + `$TMPDIR`/`/private/tmp` + the `~/.claude` state dirs + the stage's own build-cache root and, for a Claude stage, its own temp dir (+ the `~/.claude.json` state file via `(literal …)`). **`~/.claude` is narrowed to Claude Code's own state (#774):** a stage writes only `projects/` (session transcripts, which `--resume` needs), `sessions/`, `session-env/`, `shell-snapshots/`, `file-history/`, `tasks/`, `plans/`, `debug/`, `paste-cache/`, `backups/` and the legacy `todos/` and `statsig/` (`sandbox::CLAUDE_STATE_DIRS`, taken from Claude Code's application-data docs and a traced `claude -p` run; that trace was on Linux and stopped at the first API call, so later writes come from the docs), never `~/.claude` itself, so it can't add a new entry there. Beside them it may write only the login-refresh lock files, `.oauth_refresh.lock` and `.oauth_refresh.lock.<suffix>` (`sandbox::oauth_lock_regexes`, a `file-write*` regex per `~/.claude` path, never `file-link`), so a stage can refresh an expired token, and `.credentials.json` when it already exists: granted as a writable `literal` after the same checks as `~/.claude.json` (a single-link regular file of the user's, not a symlink outside `~/.claude`), otherwise not granted, so a stage can't create it. It stays writable because a refresh that can't be saved can sign the user out. **`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is followed:** for a Claude stage, `cli_runner` reads it as the stage sees it (`stage_env_value`) and keeps it only when absolute (`sandbox::claude_config_dir`; a relative value is named on the launch line and `~/.claude` is used). When set, the state dirs, lock files, `.credentials.json`, `<config>/.claude.json` (instead of `~/.claude.json`), the `projects` auto-memory deny and the state file's link check all use that dir instead of `~/.claude`, and `ensure_home_roots` creates it (its last component only) and its state dirs. The config dir must pass the same checks as a system root (`resolve_system_root`, owner-checked; `~/.claude` too); one that fails, such as `$HOME` itself or a dir under `~/.config`, is left out with its state dirs, files and lock files, and named on the launch line. In-process tools (`chat_engine`) pass none and keep `~/.claude`. After every allow, `sandbox::claude_config_denies` denies, for `~/.claude` and (when set) the `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, each as given and as its realpath: the dir itself as a path; the dirs Claude Code loads as instructions, config or code or keeps installs in (`skills/`, `agents/`, `commands/`, `plugins/`, `hooks/`, `rules/`, `output-styles/`, `workflows/`, `agent-memory/`, `themes/`, `ide/`, `jobs/`, `daemon/`, `local/`, `mods/`, `dev-mods/`); the files `settings.json`, `settings.local.json`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `keybindings.json`, `remote-settings.json`, `mcp.json`, `.config.json` and `policy-limits.json` with its sidecars; and every project's auto memory (`projects/*/memory`). A sandboxed Claude stage runs with `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`, so the CLI doesn't create a memory dir it can't write. The CLI keeps its macOS login in the Keychain, which the profile neither grants nor changes. **A Codex writer stage gets its own `CODEX_HOME` (#784; not yet checked with a real `codex exec` on a Mac):** Codex writes its session rollouts, thread-writer locks, `.tmp`, logs and state DBs under `CODEX_HOME` at start, and a failed rollout or writer lock is fatal, so a Codex writer stage in a sandboxed mission (fresh and resumed) runs with `CODEX_HOME` and `CODEX_SQLITE_HOME` set to its own home, `~/Library/Caches/octopush/codex-home/<workspace>/<mode>` (`sandbox::prepare_codex_home`, keyed like its build-cache root, so a readonly mission never shares a writer's sessions and a resumed stage finds its own), plus `-c sqlite_home="<home>"` and `-c log_dir="<home>/log"` (`sandbox::codex_home_overrides`), so a `sqlite_home` or `log_dir` in the user's `config.toml` can't put state shared by every workspace somewhere else (Codex ignores config keys it doesn't know). The user's `~/.codex` (or login-shell `CODEX_HOME`) is never a write root. Octopush makes the home outside the sandbox before each launch with the build cache's checks (`ensure_cache_root`: `O_NOFOLLOW`, owner check, 0700; a home swapped for a link fails the stage and its target is never chmodded), creates and pins `.tmp` in it, removes any entry the profile denies (`sandbox::purge_denied_entries`), and copies the user's `config.toml` into it as a read-only (0400) file: written in the home's parent, which no stage can write, created fresh with `O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW`, then renamed into place, so a link at the name is replaced, never written through; a config the user removed is removed from the copy. The profile grants the home as a subtree and denies, after every allow (`sandbox::codex_home_rules`, `file-write*` and `file-link`): the home dir itself and its `.tmp` (neither can be renamed, removed or replaced by a link), and, in the home and in the user's Codex home (as given and as its realpath), what an audit of Codex's source found it reads back as config, instructions, credentials, env, model metadata, managed config, plugins or tool catalogs: every top-level `*.toml` (`config.toml`, `managed_config.toml`, `requirements.toml`, `environments.toml`, `<profile>.config.toml`), `auth.json`, `AGENTS.md`, `AGENTS.override.md`, `instructions.md`, `hooks.json`, `.env`, `models_cache.json` (it carries each model's system prompt), `cloud-config-bundle-cache.json`, every `managed-config-<ns>.json`, `.tmp/plugins.sha`, `.tmp/plugin-share-local-paths-v1.json`, and the dirs `prompts/`, `rules/`, `skills/`, `migrated-command-skills/`, `memories/`, `memories_v2/`, `memories_extensions/`, `plugins/`, `hooks/`, `agents/`, `secrets/`, `cache/`, `packages/`, `proxy/`, `.tmp/marketplaces/` and `.tmp/plugins/`. Every name is matched case-insensitively (each ASCII letter as both cases, `k` and `s` also as the Kelvin sign and the long s; `sandbox::ci_regex`), because the volume is case-insensitive. Codex's own writes to those (its bundled skills into `skills/.system`, the curated-plugin sync, tool-catalog caches, the models cache) are then refused, which Codex logs and survives.
